claim: C. elegans males exhibit a period of reduced activity following ejaculation.
source: Similar to other species, C. elegans males exhibit a period of reduced activity following ejaculation (Barfield and Geyer, 1972; Oomura et al., 1983; Ureshi et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work on other species and is stated as a finding in C. elegans.

claim: Within 2 min after being placed on a bacterial lawn containing 15 immobile hermaphrodites, 1-day-old virgin males commenced mating and inserted their spicules into the hermaphrodites.
source: Within 2 min after being placed on a 5 mm diameter bacterial lawn containing 15 immobile hermaphrodites, 1-day-old virgin males commenced mating and inserted their spicules into the hermaphrodites (Figure 1B, Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: Following ejaculation, approximately 12 min (SD = ±6 min 30 s) passed before males intromit their spicules again.
source: However following ejaculation, ∼12 min (SD = ±6 min 30 s) passed before they intromit their spicules again (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The interval from the 1st spicule insertion to the 2nd spicule insertion is referred to as the 'refractory period'.
source: Thus, we conservatively refer to the interval from the 1st spicule insertion to the 2nd spicule insertion as the 'refractory period'.
evidence: This is a definition provided by the authors based on their observations.

claim: Within 34 s after introduction to the mating lawn, virgin males placed their tail on the hermaphrodite cuticle and began searching for the vulva.
source: Within 34 s after introduction to the mating lawn, virgin males placed their tail on the hermaphrodite cuticle and began searching for the vulva (Figure 3B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Following intromission, males kept their spicules inserted for an average of 94 s.
source: following intromission, they kept their spicules inserted for an average of 94 s.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental measurements during mating behavior.

claim: After spicule retraction, approximately 5 min passed before the males re-executed copulation.
source: After spicule retraction, ∼5 min passed before the males re-executed copulation (Figure 3B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Male sexual drive was temporarily suppressed after spicule retraction.
source: After spicule retraction, ∼5 min passed before the males re-executed copulation (Figure 3B), indicating that male sexual drive was temporarily suppressed.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed delay in re-mating behavior.

claim: The number of times males passed over the vulva was significantly increased during the 2nd mating bout compared to the 1st.
source: however, the number of times they passed over the vulva was significantly increased (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Various male sensory-motor circuits recover differentially to the source(s) that attenuate mating behavior after ejaculation.
source: These observations indicate that various male sensory-motor circuits recover differentially to the source(s) that attenuate mating behavior after ejaculation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential recovery of mating behaviors.

claim: Males with a longer refractory period (9 to 30 min) were more successful in siring progeny than males with shorter refractory periods (3 to 8:59 min).
source: We found that males with a longer refractory period were more successful in siring progeny than their counterparts, whose refractory periods were shorter than 9 min (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by progeny count data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Males from both refractory period groups did not display a difference in the amount of progeny they sired during the 1st mating.
source: Importantly, males from both groups did not display a difference in the amount of progeny they sired during the 1st mating (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by progeny count data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: A longer refractory period allows males to recover their ability to sire progeny.
source: Thus, a longer refractory period allows males to recover their ability to sire progeny.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that males with longer refractory periods sired more progeny in the 2nd mating.

claim: Males lacking all gonad structures required longer time to commence mating.
source: We found that males lacking all of these structures required longer time to commence mating (Figure 3F)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from laser-ablation experiments shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The gonad sends a signal to promote mating behavior.
source: We found that males lacking all of these structures required longer time to commence mating (Figure 3F), implying that the gonad sends a signal to promote this behavior.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that gonad-ablated males take longer to commence mating.

claim: After gonad-ablated males inserted and retracted their spicules, their refractory period was similar to the mock-ablated control.
source: After the operated males inserted and retracted their spicules, their refractory period was similar to the mock-ablated control and coincidentally similar to the time required for their 1st spicule insertion (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Germ line-ablated males behaviorally resembled the gonad-ablated males.
source: We found that germ line-ablated males behaviorally resembled the gonad-ablated males (Figure 3F,G)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3F and 3G.

claim: The germ line is required for the gonad to promote mating.
source: We found that germ line-ablated males behaviorally resembled the gonad-ablated males (Figure 3F,G), indicating that the germ line is required for the gonad to promote mating.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the similarity in behavior between germ line-ablated and gonad-ablated males.

claim: Preventing sperm release by linker cell ablation increased the duration of the refractory period, relative to the mock-ablated control.
source: However, as a population of operated males, preventing sperm release increased the duration of the refractory period, relative to the mock-ablated control (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The duration of the refractory period is plastic and could be modified by cellular components that directly or indirectly sense sperm release.
source: This suggests that the duration of the refractory period is plastic and could be modified by cellular components that directly or indirectly sense sperm release.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that some linker cell-ablated males compensated for lack of sperm movement while others did not.

claim: Each spicule contains the sensory dendrites of two neurons, the bilateral left/right SPV and SPD.
source: In addition, each spicule contains the sensory dendrites of two neurons, the bilateral left/right SPV and SPD (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is based on established anatomical knowledge and is illustrated in Figure 2C.

claim: SPV and SPD neurons send a process down the shaft of the spicule and have ciliated sensory endings that are exposed to the environment at the spicule tip.
source: These neurons send a process down the shaft of the spicule and have ciliated sensory endings that are exposed to the environment at the spicule tip.
evidence: The claim is based on established anatomical knowledge cited from Sulston et al. (1980).

claim: Laser-ablation of SPV and SPD neurons during L4 resulted in males with variable mating problems including failure to follow through the steps of mating, failure to insert their spicules, and failure to ejaculate or prematurely ejaculating sperm prior to intromission.
source: When we laser-ablated these neurons during L4, the resulting males had variable mating problems. These defects include failure to follow through the steps of mating, failure to insert their spicules, and failure to ejaculate or prematurely ejaculating sperm prior to intromission (Figure 4A)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and is consistent with previously reported defects.

claim: Spicule tip cut adult males did not display variable mating defects unlike larval SPD and SPV-ablated males.
source: Unlike the larval SPD and SPV-ablated males, spicule tip cut adult males did not display variable mating defects (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Both mock-cut control and spicule tips-cut males displayed normal initial response times to hermaphrodites.
source: Both the mock-cut control and operated males displayed normal initial response times to hermaphrodites (Figure 3F)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Spicule tips-cut males displayed a significantly shorter refractory period than control males (296 ± 217 s vs 499 ± 224 s, p value=0.0121).
source: but interestingly, the spicule tips-cut males displayed a significantly shorter refractory period than control males (296 ± 217 s vs 499 ± 224 s, p value=0.0121, Mann–Whitney test) (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G with statistical analysis.

claim: In wild-type males, the spicule sensilla modify the duration of the refractory period.
source: This suggests that in wild-type males, the spicule sensilla modify the duration of the refractory period.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that spicule tips-cut males have shorter refractory periods.

claim: In approximately half of the spicule tips-cut males, the valve region opened (12/13 control vs 8/15 ablated, p=0.0377).
source: In approximately half of the spicule tips-cut males, the valve region opened (12/13 control vs 8/15 ablated, p=0.0377, Fisher's exact test)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Sperm rarely passed out of the cloaca into the hermaphrodite in spicule tips-cut males (10/14 control vs 1/15 ablated, p=0.0005).
source: but sperm rarely passed out of the cloaca into the hermaphrodite (10/14 control vs 1/15 ablated, p=0.0005, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: 67% of control males sired progeny at the 1st mating and 33% of males sired progeny at the second mating (n = 12).
source: 67% of control males sired progeny at the 1st mating and 33% of males sired progeny at the second mating (n = 12) (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: No spicule tips-cut males were successful at siring progeny at the 1st insert, and only two were successful the 2nd time (n = 12).
source: No operated males were successful at the 1st insert, and only two were successful the 2nd time (n = 12) (Figure 4B; Liu and Sternberg, 1995; Schindelman et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and is consistent with previously reported findings.

claim: The putative sensory function of the spicules promotes both sperm movement and affects the refractory period.
source: Thus, the putative sensory function of the spicules promotes both sperm movement and affects the refractory period.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observations on spicule tips-cut males.

claim: Many spicule tips-cut males inserted and retracted their spicules multiple times during the 2nd mating, with each penetration lasting only a few seconds.
source: However, we noticed this difference became exaggerated during the 2nd mating. Generally, a male maintains spicule insertion throughout the sperm transfer process, which normally takes longer than 30 s. In contrast, many of the mating-experienced cut males inserted and retracted their spicules multiple times, with each penetration lasting only a few seconds (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Spicule tips-cut males were defective in either entering or maintaining the ejaculatory state.
source: This observation indicated that the spicule tips-cut males were defective in either entering or maintaining the ejaculatory state.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that spicule tips-cut males inserted and retracted multiple times.

claim: After spicule insertion, Ca2+ transients in SPV and SPD neurons gradually increased; the average peak activity occurred approximately 4 s post intromission.
source: After spicule insertion, Ca2+ transients in these cells gradually increased; the average peak activity occurred ∼4 s post intromission.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Ca2+ transients in SPV and SPD began to decline during the sperm's movement through the vas deferens and continued to decrease after sperm release (n = 5, Figure 5A; Table 1; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
source: The Ca2+ transients began to decline during the sperm's movement through the vas deferens and continued to decrease after sperm release (n = 5, Figure 5A; Table 1; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5A, Table 1, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Coincident with full spicule penetration, Ca2+ transients rapidly increased in the SPC.
source: Coincident with full spicule penetration, Ca2+ transients rapidly increased in the SPC.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The peak G-CaMP fluorescence intensity in SPC occurred faster than in the SPV and SPD neurons (1.3 s vs 4.0 s, p<0.05, ANOVA, Figure 4B; Table 1; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
source: The peak G-CaMP fluorescence intensity occurred faster than in the SPV and SPD neurons (1.3 s vs 4.0 s, p<0.05, ANOVA, Figure 4B; Table 1; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4B, Table 1, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis.

claim: Ca2+ transients in the SPC began to decrease during sperm movement into the gonadal vas deferens.
source: However, similar to the SPV and SPD, the Ca2+ transients in the SPC began to decrease during sperm movement into the gonadal vas deferens (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The ACh agonist oxotremorine S (OxoS) induces males to protrude their spicules and some males to ejaculate.
source: The potentially non-specific ACh agonist oxotremorine S (OxoS) induces males to protrude their spicules and some males to ejaculate.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations with OxoS treatment.

claim: Males exposed to OxoS showed increases in gonadal Ca2+ transients (n = 5).
source: We saw increases in gonadal Ca2+ transients in males (n = 5) that were exposed to the agonist (Figure 5C)
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The somatic gonad activity can be stimulated by ACh.
source: We saw increases in gonadal Ca2+ transients in males (n = 5) that were exposed to the agonist (Figure 5C), indicating that the somatic gonad activity can be stimulated by ACh.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that OxoS, an ACh agonist, induces gonadal Ca2+ transients.

claim: Immediately upon spicule insertion, the valve's Ca2+ transients reached their peak (approximately 1.8 s) with kinetics similar to the SPC neurons.
source: Immediately upon spicule insertion, we measured that the valve's Ca2+ transients reached their peak (∼1.8 s) with kinetics similar to the SPC neurons (Figure 5D; Table 1; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5D, Table 1, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ca2+ transients remained high in the valve until it opened, on average 6.9 ± 1.5 s after insertion (n = 7).
source: Ca2+ transients remained high in the valve until it opened, on average 6.9 ± 1.5 s after insertion (n = 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data.

claim: When sperm moved through the vas deferens, the level of Ca2+ transients in the valve began to slowly decrease.
source: When sperm moved through the vas deferens, the level of Ca2+ transients in the valve began to slowly decrease (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: In spicule-tips cut males, the valve displayed a rapid increase in Ca2+ transients similar to mock-cut males.
source: Similar to the mock-cut males, the valve in spicule-tips cut males displayed a rapid increase in Ca2+ transients (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: In spicule-tips cut males, the decrease in Ca2+ transients in the valve was more gradual and protracted compared to mock-cut males.
source: But instead of a distinct decrease in Ca2+ transients that coincide with the opening of the valve and sperm movement, the decrease in Ca2+ transients was more gradual and protracted (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figures 5E and 5F.

claim: The valve did not open in 10/19 spicule-tips cut males (compared to 18/19 controls, p value=0.0078).
source: Coincident with the altered activity profiles, the valve did not open in 10/19 males (compared to 18/19 controls, p value=0.0078, Fisher's exact test)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: In spicule-tips cut males, sperm was not transferred to the hermaphrodite in the remaining males where the valve opened.
source: and in the remaining males, sperm was not transferred to the hermaphrodite.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: Nearly all mock-cut controls released sperm into their mates (1/19 ablated vs 18/19 controls, p value<0.0001).
source: In contrast, nearly all mock-cut controls released sperm into their mates (1/19 ablated vs 18/19 controls, p value<0.0001, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Immediately upon intromission, the SPC primes the gonad for the initiation of ejaculation.
source: the Ca2+ imaging suggests that immediately upon intromission, the SPC primes the gonad for the initiation of ejaculation
evidence: The claim is inferred from calcium imaging data showing coordinated activity of SPC and the gonad.

claim: The spicule sensory neurons provide further stimulation necessary for sperm movement and release.
source: and the spicule sensory neurons provide further stimulation necessary for sperm movement and release.
evidence: The claim is inferred from calcium imaging and ablation data.

claim: None of the transgenic males expressing ChR2 from Pgar-3b, Punc-103B, Punc-17, or Punc-17S initiated ejaculation or released sperm upon stimulation.
source: We found that none of the transgenic males expressing ChR2 initiated ejaculation or released sperm upon stimulation (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Transgenic males simultaneously expressing Punc-103B:ChR2, Punc-17S:ChR2, and Pgar-3B:ChR2 did ejaculate upon light stimulation.
source: However, transgenic males simultaneously expressing Punc-103B:ChR2, Punc-17S:ChR2, and Pgar-3B:ChR2 did ejaculate upon light stimulation (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A larger number of cells than expected, which includes the SPD, SPC, PCA, and PCB neurons, as well as sex-shared head and ventral cord neurons and sex muscles, must be stimulated to initiate ejaculation and release sperm.
source: This indicated that a larger number of cells than we expected, which includes the SPD, SPC, PCA, and PCB neurons, as well as sex-shared head and ventral cord neurons and sex muscles, must be stimulated to initiate ejaculation and release sperm (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the optogenetic experiments showing that multiple promoters are needed to induce ejaculation.

claim: Ablating SPV/SPD and SPC neurons singly slightly reduced the ejaculation efficiency, but not enough to be statistically significant (p value=0.78 and 0.42, respectively).
source: We killed the SPV/SPD and SPC neurons singly and found that these treatments slightly reduced the ejaculation efficiency, but not enough to be statistically significant (p value=0.78 and 0.42, respectively, Fisher's exact test) (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis.

claim: Ablating the PCB singly reduced the ejaculation efficiency, but not enough to be statistically significant (p value=0.2).
source: We found that ablating the PCB singly reduced the ejaculation efficiency, but like the SPC neurons, not enough to be statistically significant (p value=0.2, Fisher's exact test) (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B with statistical analysis.

claim: Ablating both SPC and PCB significantly reduced the number of males that released sperm compared to the mock-ablated control (42%, p=0.013).
source: However, compared to the mock-ablated control, ablating both SPC and PCB significantly reduced the number of males that released sperm (42%, p=0.013, Fisher's exact test) (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B with statistical analysis.

claim: There was no obvious decrease in ejaculation behavior when comparing SPC/PCB/PCC to SPC/PCB ablated males (p value=0.37).
source: However, we did not see any obvious decrease in ejaculation behavior when comparing SPC/PCB/PCC to SPC/PCB ablated males (p value=0.37, Fisher's exact test) (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B with statistical analysis.

claim: Few PCA-ablated males were able to ejaculate after stimulation (16%, p value=0.0003).
source: To our surprise, we observed that few PCA-ablated males were able to ejaculate after stimulation (16%, p value=0.0003, Fisher's exact test) (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B with statistical analysis.

claim: PCA neurons play a role in promoting ejaculation.
source: This uncovered a role for the PCA in promoting ejaculation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that PCA-ablated males rarely ejaculate after ChR2 stimulation.

claim: The sex muscles displayed a peak in Ca2+ transients immediately upon spicule intromission.
source: As expected, the sex muscles displayed a peak in Ca2+ transients immediately upon spicule intromission (Table 1; Figure 7A,B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Table 1, Figures 7A and 7B, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Coincident with the initiation of ejaculation, approximately 11 s later, the gubernaculum and anal depressor muscles displayed an increase in Ca2+ transients and became hyper-contracted.
source: Coincident with the initiation of ejaculation, ∼11 s later, the gubernaculum and anal depressor muscles displayed an increase in Ca2+ transients and became hyper-contracted (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Table 1.

claim: After approximately 15 to 20 s, sperm was detected in the hermaphrodite uterus.
source: After ∼15 to 20 s, we detected sperm in the hermaphrodite uterus.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations during calcium imaging.

claim: When sperm transfer was completed, the Ca2+ transients in the muscles began to oscillate as they dampened.
source: When sperm transfer was completed, the Ca2+ transients in the muscles began to oscillate as they dampened (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The PCA Ca2+ transients gradually increased after spicule insertion with their first peak at 6.3 ± 0.56 s post intromission (n = 5).
source: We found that the PCA Ca2+ transients gradually increased after spicule insertion with their first peak at 6.3 ± 0.56 s post intromission (n = 5, Table 1; Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Table 1, Figure 7C, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Elevated Ca2+ transients in PCA lasted after sperm release, unlike the SPC and the SPV/SPD.
source: but unlike the SPC and the SPV/SPD, elevated Ca2+ transients lasted after sperm release (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The timing of the peak PCA Ca2+ transients (9.2 ± 2.9 s) proceeded and overlapped with the second Ca2+ increase in the gubernaculum erector and retractor and anal depressor muscles (11 ± 3.9 s, p value=0.8).
source: The timing of the peak PCA Ca2+ transients (9.2 ± 2.9 s) proceeded and overlapped with the second Ca2+ increase in the gubernaculum erector and retractor and anal depressor muscles (11 ± 3.9 s, p value=0.8, Mann–Whitney t test compared to PCA peak)
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data with statistical analysis.

claim: PCA is promoting changes in the gubernaculum muscles.
source: The timing of the peak PCA Ca2+ transients (9.2 ± 2.9 s) proceeded and overlapped with the second Ca2+ increase in the gubernaculum erector and retractor and anal depressor muscles (11 ± 3.9 s, p value=0.8, Mann–Whitney t test compared to PCA peak), suggesting PCA is promoting these changes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the temporal correlation of Ca2+ transients in PCA and the gubernaculum muscles.

claim: Laser-ablation of the PCA did not have gross effects on vulva location behavior, spicule intromission, or ejaculation.
source: However, laser-ablation of the PCA did not have gross effects on vulva location behavior, spicule intromission, or ejaculation.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations and is consistent with previously reported findings.

claim: The PCB and PCC neurons can compensate for the damaged PCA cells in operated males.
source: Likely, the PCB and PCC neurons can compensate for the damaged cells in operated males (Liu and Sternberg, 1995; Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of gross defects in PCA-ablated males and is consistent with previously reported redundancy.

claim: Removing the SPV/SPD neurons did not affect PCA or dorsal sex muscle activity.
source: Removing the SPV/SPD neurons did not affect PCA or dorsal sex muscle activity (Figure 8A,B, Figure 8—figure supplements 1, 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figures 8A and 8B, and Figure 8—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: PCA and its targets are not downstream of SPV/SPD.
source: Thus, PCA and its targets are not downstream of SPV/SPD.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that removing SPV/SPD does not affect PCA activity.

claim: When SPV/SPD were removed, the increases in SPC Ca2+ transients occurred at a slower rate.
source: In contrast, when SPV/SPD were removed, the increases occurred at a slower rate (Table 1; Figure 8C,D, Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Table 1, Figures 8C and 8D, and Figure 8—figure supplement 3.

claim: The SPV/SPD are promoting SPC activity upon insertion.
source: This suggests that the SPV/SPD are promoting SPC activity upon insertion.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that SPC Ca2+ transients increase more slowly when SPV/SPD are removed.

claim: Ca2+ transients in the PCB displayed minor increases upon insertion, and their activity quickly dissipated.
source: Ca2+ transients in the PCB displayed minor increases upon insertion, and their activity quickly dissipated (Figure 8—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 4.

claim: PCB activity was unaffected by SPV/SPD removal.
source: This activity was unaffected by SPV/SPD removal (Figure 8E, Figure 8—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8E and Figure 8—figure supplement 4.

claim: PCB does not play a significant role after insertion.
source: This result suggests that PCB does not play a significant role after insertion.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that PCB activity quickly dissipates after insertion.

claim: In SPC-ablated males, the PCB can compensate for the loss of the SPC and promote 475 nm wavelength light-induced ejaculation in ChR2-expressing males.
source: We propose that in SPC-ablated males, the PCB can compensate for the loss of the SPC and promote 475 nm wavelength light-induced ejaculation in ChR2-expressing males.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that ablating both SPC and PCB is needed to significantly reduce ejaculation.

claim: Laser-ablation of all eight spicule socket cell nuclei in adult males did not affect insertion (11 out of 27 control mock-ablated males could insert, compared to 7/22 ablated males, p value=0.6).
source: We found that insertion was unaffected (11 out of 27 control mock-ablated males could insert, compared to 7/22 ablated males, p value=0.6, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Only 1/7 socket cell-ablated males released sperm into the hermaphrodite for ≥10 s; the other ablated males showed variable dysfunctions in executing or sustaining sperm release.
source: However, only 1/7 ablated males released sperm into the hermaphrodite for ≥10 s; the other ablated males showed variable dysfunctions in executing or sustaining sperm release.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: 73% (n = 8/11) of mock-ablated males released sperm into the hermaphrodite for ≥10 s (p value=0.0498).
source: In contrast, 73% (n = 8/11) of mock-ablated males released sperm into the hermaphrodite for ≥10 s (p value=0.0498, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The socket cells promote sperm release.
source: Thus, similar to cutting off the spicule tips, ejaculation was significantly reduced, indicating that the socket cells promote sperm release.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that socket cell-ablated males have reduced sperm release.

claim: Removing the SPV and SPD in conjunction with the socket cells had a more significant impact on mating behavior than removing socket cells alone.
source: Thus, removing the SPV and SPD in conjunction with the socket cells had a more significant impact on mating behavior.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparing the effects of socket cell ablation versus spicule tip cutting.

claim: Socket cell Ca2+ transients increased rapidly upon insertion, with a profile similar to the SPC and the gonadal valve.
source: We found that socket cell Ca2+ transients increased rapidly upon insertion, with a profile similar to the SPC and the gonadal valve (Table 1; Figure 9A, Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Table 1, Figure 9A, and Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ca2+ transients in socket cells then declined to about half their peak intensity at the time of sperm release.
source: Ca2+ transients then declined to about half their peak intensity at the time of sperm release (Figure 9A).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The socket cells are directly involved in ejaculatory behaviors.
source: This supports the hypothesis that the socket cells are directly involved in ejaculatory behaviors.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that socket cells show Ca2+ transients during mating.

claim: The enzyme necessary to make DA, tyrosine hydroxylase (cat-2), in addition to aromatic amino acid decarboxylase (bas-1), is expressed in the socket cells.
source: Intriguingly, the enzyme necessary to make DA, tyrosine hydroxylase (cat-2), in addition to aromatic amino acid decarboxylase (bas-1), is also expressed in these neuronal support cells (Figure 9—figure supplement 1; Lints and Emmons, 1999; Hare and Loer, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by expression data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1 and is consistent with previously reported findings.

claim: In contrast to the socket cells, the DA-expressing rays R5A, R7A, and R9A exhibited no gross changes in Ca2+ transients after spicule insertion.
source: We found that in contrast to the socket cells, these neurons exhibited no gross changes in Ca2+ transients after spicule insertion (Figure 9B, Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 9B and Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claim: If DA promotes ejaculation, its source would be the socket cells, not the ray neurons.
source: This suggests that if DA promotes ejaculation, its source would be the socket cells, not the ray neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that socket cells, but not ray neurons, show Ca2+ transients during ejaculation.

claim: Many cat-2(lf) mutant males had difficulty releasing sperm or sustaining sperm release into the hermaphrodite; some males even displayed 'coitus interruptus'.
source: Many mutant males had difficulty releasing sperm or sustaining sperm release into the hermaphrodite; some males even displayed 'coitus interruptus', by pulling out their spicules from the hermaphrodite and then erratically releasing sperm onto the media.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of cat-2(lf) mutant males.

claim: 79% of wild-type males successfully transferred sperm for at least 10 s, compared to only 31% of cat-2(lf) males (p=0.02).
source: When we measured if the males can sustain sperm release into the hermaphrodite for at least 10 s, 79% of wild-type males successfully transferred sperm, compared to only 31% of cat-2(lf) males (p=0.02, Fisher's exact test, Figure 9C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9C with statistical analysis.

claim: Adult cat-2(lf) males exhibit reduced ectopic intromission attempts in response to exogenous DA.
source: As expected, adult cat-2(lf) males exhibit reduced ectopic intromission attempts in response to exogenous DA (Figure 9D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9D and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: Exogenously applied DA did not restore the ability to transfer sperm in cat-2(lf) males.
source: However interestingly, exogenously applied DA did not restore the ability to transfer sperm (Figure 9C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Expressing cat-2(+) in the dopaminergic rays and socket cells using the Pcat-2 promoter rescued both ectopic intromission attempts and ejaculation defects.
source: To determine which dopaminergic cells promoted sperm release, we expressed cat-2(+) in the dopaminergic rays and socket cells using the Pcat-2 promoter; this construct rescued both ectopic intromission attempts and ejaculation defects (Figure 9C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 9C and 9D.

claim: Using the Pdat-1 promoter to express cat-2 in ray neurons, but not in the spicule socket cells, suppressed ectopic intromission attempts to wild-type levels but sperm transfer remained abnormal.
source: We next used the Pdat-1 promoter to express cat-2 in ray neurons, but not in the spicule socket cells. Similar to exogenous DA exposure, ectopic intromission attempts were suppressed to wild-type levels (Figure 9D), but sperm transfer remained abnormal (Figure 9C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 9C and 9D.

claim: DA synthesis in the socket cells is necessary for sperm release in C. elegans males.
source: Thus, DA synthesis in the socket cells is necessary for sperm release in C. elegans males.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that expressing cat-2 in socket cells rescues sperm release defects.

claim: During the first mating, transgenic cat-2(lf) males expressing cat-2(+) in the ray neurons and spicule socket cells, or just in the ray neurons commenced mating in a similar time frame (51 s vs 121 s, p value=0.08).
source: We found that during the first mating, transgenic cat-2(lf) males expressing cat-2(+) in the ray neurons and spicule socket cells, or just in the ray neurons commenced mating in a similar time frame (51 s vs 121 s, p value=0.08, Mann–Whitney test) (Figure 9E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9E with statistical analysis.

claim: Transgenic males that lacked cat-2(+) in the socket cells had shorter refractory periods, relative to males with cat-2(+)-containing socket cells (518 s vs 1083 s, p value=0.0127).
source: However, transgenic males that lacked cat-2(+) in the socket cells had shorter refractory periods, relative to males with cat-2(+)-containing socket cells (518 s vs 1083 s, p value=0.0127, Mann–Whitney test) (Figure 9E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9E with statistical analysis.

claim: DA contributes to the refractory period length.
source: Thus, DA contributes to the refractory period length.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that males lacking DA in socket cells have shorter refractory periods.

claim: While concentrations of 15 and 20 mM DA slowed down the time it takes a male to insert his spicules, the difference was not statistically significant.
source: We found that while concentrations of 15 and 20 mM DA slowed down the time it takes a male to insert his spicules, the difference was not statistically significant (Figure 9F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9F.

claim: 25 mM DA induces a significant increase in the time required for males to insert their spicules.
source: However, 25 mM DA induces a significant increase in the time required for males to insert their spicules (Figure 9F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9F.

claim: Few males were successful in inserting their spicules within 5 min when exposed to 25 mM DA.
source: Indeed, few males were successful in inserting their spicules within this time frame.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations with 25 mM DA treatment.

claim: The decreased mating ability on 25 mM DA was not due to sluggish movement or paralysis.
source: This decreased mating ability was not due to sluggish movement or paralysis, as they still commenced mating in a similar, but slightly longer timeframe (Figure 9—figure supplement 1) and their backing velocity along the hermaphrodite remained the same (171 ± 43 µm/s n = 6 control, 178 ± 35 µm/s n = 5 25 mM DA).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1 and velocity measurements.

claim: Exogenous DA is capable of interfering with males' mating ability.
source: Thus, exogenous DA is capable of interfering with males' mating ability.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that high concentrations of DA delay spicule insertion.

claim: C. elegans males display an average lifespan of 12 days, show significant decline in sexual function at day 3, and are unable to sire progeny by day 5.
source: C. elegans males display an average lifespan of 12 days, show significant decline in sexual function at day 3, and are unable to sire progeny by day 5 (Gems and Riddle, 1996; Guo et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A longer refractory period allows males to recover their ability to transfer sperm.
source: We discovered that a longer refractory period allows males to recover their ability to transfer sperm.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations showing that males with longer refractory periods sire more progeny.

claim: When males attempt to mate again too quickly, their ability to sire progeny is reduced.
source: When males attempt to mate again too quickly, their ability to sire progeny is reduced.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations showing that males with shorter refractory periods sire fewer progeny.

claim: The period of reduced activity and ability following ejaculation may help insure that the male copulates with different partners.
source: Thus, the period of reduced activity and ability we observed following ejaculation may help insure that the male copulates with different partners (Figure 10A).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis inferred from the observation that the refractory period prevents immediate re-mating with the same partner.

claim: The refractory period is dependent upon the males' ability to produce and sense successful ejaculation.
source: We determined that the refractory period is dependent upon the males' ability to produce and sense successful ejaculation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental observations showing that disrupting ejaculation affects the refractory period.

claim: SPV and SPD sense the intrauterine environment, promote sperm release, and regulate the refractory period.
source: We propose that SPV and SPD sense the intrauterine environment, promote sperm release, and regulate the refractory period.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on experimental observations of SPV and SPD function.

claim: The SPC neurons, with support from the SPV/SPD neurons and the post cloacal sensilla, trigger the initiation of ejaculation.
source: Our data indicate that the SPC neurons, with support from the SPV/SPD neurons and the post cloacal sensilla, trigger the initiation of ejaculation (Figure 10B).
evidence: The claim is inferred from calcium imaging and optogenetic data.

claim: The SPC, via direct cholinergic signaling to the gonad, triggers the initiation of ejaculation.
source: We propose a model where the SPC, via direct cholinergic signaling to the gonad (Jarrell et al., 2012), triggers the initiation of ejaculation (Figure 10B).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on calcium imaging data and connectome information.

claim: The SPV and SPD help maintain a lower threshold in the SPC, allowing the SPC to trigger spicule intromission without inducing premature ejaculation.
source: We propose that the SPV and SPD help maintain a lower threshold in the SPC, allowing the SPC to trigger spicule intromission without inducing premature ejaculation.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the observation that SPC activity is reduced when SPV/SPD are removed.

claim: The gubernaculum erector and retractor muscles, and possibly the anal depressor, are involved in the penultimate step of male mating.
source: Calcium imaging data presented in this work and ablation data in previous work suggest that the gubernaculum erector and retractor muscles, and possibly the anal depressor, are involved in the penultimate step of male mating (Figure 10B).
evidence: The claim is inferred from calcium imaging data and previous ablation studies.

claim: The gubernaculum muscles contract to facilitate sperm release, likely by re-adjusting the spicules' position.
source: Together, these data indicate that the gubernaculum muscles contract to facilitate sperm release, likely by re-adjusting the spicules' position.
evidence: The claim is inferred from calcium imaging data and previous ablation studies.

claim: The post cloacal sensilla PCA is partially responsible for promoting gubernacular muscle contraction.
source: Our data suggest the post cloacal sensilla PCA is partially responsible (Figure 10B).
evidence: The claim is inferred from calcium imaging and optogenetic data.

claim: Glutamate is a potential PCA neurotransmitter.
source: We identified glutamate as a potential PCA neurotransmitter
evidence: The claim is inferred from the expression of the eat-4 glutamate vesicular transporter in PCA.

claim: PCA's peak activity following intromission corresponds with gubernacular muscle contractions.
source: and showed that PCA's peak activity following intromission corresponds with gubernacular muscle contractions.
evidence: The claim is based on calcium imaging data showing temporal correlation.

claim: ChR2-expressing males were unable to ectopically ejaculate when PCA was removed.
source: Additionally, we showed that ChR2-expressing males were unable to ectopically ejaculate when PCA was removed.
evidence: The claim is based on optogenetic experiments.

claim: The PCB and PCC can compensate for the loss of the PCA.
source: While ablating the PCA in a wild type mating background does not affect sperm transfer (Liu and Sternberg, 1995; Liu et al., 2011), we propose this is due to the ability of the other p.c.s. neurons, the PCB and PCC, which make similar muscular connections (Jarrell et al., 2012), to compensate for the loss of the PCA.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on connectome data and previous ablation studies.

claim: The sex muscle contractions facilitated by the PCA and other neurons are a necessary component of sperm release.
source: Thus, the sex muscle contractions facilitated by the PCA and other neurons are a necessary component of sperm release.
evidence: The claim is inferred from calcium imaging and optogenetic data.

claim: PCA activity and gubernaculum sex muscle contractions are insufficient for sperm release into the uterus.
source: However, PCA activity and gubernaculum sex muscle contractions are insufficient for sperm release into the uterus.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that males with normal PCA activity still fail to transfer sperm when SPV/SPD and socket cells are removed.

claim: The SPV/SPD neurons are involved in sperm initiation and possibly release.
source: Our data indicate that the SPV/SPD neurons are involved in sperm initiation and possibly release
evidence: The claim is inferred from calcium imaging and ablation data.

claim: The DA-expressing socket cells play no role in initiation but are required for sperm release.
source: while the DA-expressing socket cells play no role in initiation but are required for sperm release (Figure 10B).
evidence: The claim is inferred from calcium imaging and ablation data.

claim: Removal of the socket cells themselves or their ability to produce DA results in impaired sperm release.
source: Removal of the socket cells themselves or their ability to produce DA results in impaired sperm release.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations from ablation and genetic studies.

claim: The role of DA in promoting ejaculation could represent a general theme of monoaminergic modulation of sexual motor acts.
source: This role of DA could represent a general theme of monoaminergic modulation of sexual motor acts, as there is also peripheral modulation of the corpus cavernosum in mammals by monoamines, including DA and serotonin (Angulo et al., 2001; Hayes and Adaikan, 2002, d'Emmanuele di Villa Bianca et al., 2005; Senbel, 2011).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the findings in C. elegans and comparisons to mammalian systems.

claim: The socket cells represent a non-neuronal source of DA.
source: Interestingly, the socket cells represent a non-neuronal source of DA.
evidence: The claim is based on the observation that socket cells express DA synthesis enzymes but are not neurons.

claim: The socket cells in C. elegans are proposed to be invertebrate glia.
source: The socket cells in C. elegans are proposed to be invertebrate glia (Ward et al., 1975; Oikonomou and Shaham, 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on citations to previous work.

claim: Socket cell DA may function hormonally, as these cells do not express the DA re-uptake transporter.
source: Additionally, socket cell DA may function hormonally, as these cells do not express the DA re-uptake transporter.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the absence of DA re-uptake transporter expression in socket cells.

claim: Vesicles have been identified in socket cells in the hermaphrodite head, suggesting this cell type is secretory.
source: Vesicles have been identified in socket cells in the hermaphrodite head, suggesting this cell type is secretory (Doroquez et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on a citation to previous work.

claim: DA promotes the refractory period, the time between successful mating attempts, coupling sperm release with mating-related behavioral inhibition.
source: Additionally, our experiments show that DA promotes the refractory period, the time between successful mating attempts, coupling sperm release with mating-related behavioral inhibition.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations showing that DA affects the refractory period.

claim: The DA that promotes ejaculation, either humorally or synaptically, acts to reduce the activity of the post-copulatory male.
source: We propose a model where the DA that promotes ejaculation, either humorally or synaptically, acts to reduce the activity of the post-copulatory male.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the observation that DA affects both ejaculation and the refractory period.

claim: Once the effect of DA is slowly extinguished, the male is then able to mate again.
source: Once the effect of DA is slowly extinguished, the male is then able to mate again.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis about the mechanism of the refractory period.

claim: The refractory period could indirectly cause males to mate with different hermaphrodites.
source: The refractory period could indirectly cause males to mate with different hermaphrodites.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis about the function of the refractory period.

claim: The refractory period could also provide the gonad and male mating circuitry time to recover.
source: However, the refractory period could also provide the gonad and male mating circuitry time to recover, as we observed that mating drive returns before mating potency (Figure 10A).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the observation that different aspects of mating behavior recover at different rates.

claim: A large number of neurons and other cells show a dramatic increase in calcium transients upon spicule insertion.
source: Strikingly, we noticed that a large number of neurons and other cells show a dramatic increase in calcium transients upon spicule insertion.
evidence: The claim is based on calcium imaging data.

claim: The large amount of signals released near-simultaneously might compound the desensitization effect on receptors.
source: While the large amount of information contained within these signals is required for sperm release, over a period of time they may have a dampening effect on the circuitry. Many receptors undergo periods of desensitization, and the large amounts of signals released near-simultaneously might compound this effect.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis about the mechanism of circuit recovery.

claim: The re-setting of circuits could require the removal of signaling molecules that inundate the male's nervous system during copulation.
source: The re-setting of circuits could require the removal of signaling molecules that inundate the male's nervous system during copulation.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis about the mechanism of circuit recovery.

claim: Calcium transients oscillate in the sex muscles following the initiation of sperm movement.
source: Additionally, calcium transients oscillate in the sex muscles following the initiation of sperm movement.
evidence: The claim is based on calcium imaging data.

claim: The SPV and SPD neurons not only promote sperm initiation but regulate the length of the refractory period.
source: We propose that the SPV and SPD neurons not only promote sperm initiation but regulate the length of the refractory period.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on experimental observations.

claim: When SPV and SPD sensory endings enter the uterus, their activity increases and consequently sperm initiation occurs.
source: When these neurons' sensory endings enter the uterus, their activity increases and consequently sperm initiation occurs.
evidence: The claim is based on calcium imaging data.

claim: SPV and SPD activity decreases when they sense sperm release.
source: However, their activity decreases when they sense sperm release (Figure 10B).
evidence: The claim is based on calcium imaging data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: If the SPV and SPD do not sense intrauterine sperm, then their extended activity subsequently promotes the continued release of DA and other neurotransmitters.
source: If the SPV and SPD do not sense intrauterine sperm, then their extended activity subsequently promotes the continued release of DA and other neurotransmitters.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis about the mechanism of refractory period regulation.

claim: Lengthening the refractory period would allow time for the males to produce sperm if the SPV and SPD do not efficiently sense sperm in the uterine environment due to a low ejaculate sperm count.
source: Consequently, lengthening the refractory period would allow time for the males to produce sperm.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis about the function of the refractory period.

claim: In mammals, post-ejaculatory regulation of the refractory period occurs in networks in the hypothalamus, amygdala, and septal nuclei.
source: In mammals, post-ejaculatory regulation of the refractory period occurs in networks in the hypothalamus, amygdala, and septal nuclei (Gogate et al., 1995; Parfitt and Newman, 1998; Dominguez and Hull, 2010).
evidence: The claim is based on citations to previous work on mammals.

claim: The refractory period in C. elegans is modulated by the circuitry located in the male tail.
source: In contrast, we identified that the refractory period in C. elegans is modulated by the circuitry located in the male tail.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations in C. elegans.

claim: Optogenetically controlled ejaculation could not be achieved unless ChR2 was expressed in cholinergic head neurons.
source: We were unable to achieve optogenetically controlled ejaculation unless ChR2 was expressed in cholinergic head neurons.
evidence: The claim is based on optogenetic experiments.

claim: Males' sexual activities are modulated by neuronal networks that are not directly associated with the sex organs.
source: This suggests that, similar to other species, males' sexual activities are modulated by neuronal networks that are not directly associated with the sex organs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that head neurons are required for optogenetically induced ejaculation.

claim: The dorsal nerve in rats and humans that is part of the copulatory organ elicits ejaculatory responses.
source: The dorsal nerve in rats and humans that is part of the copulatory organ elicits ejaculatory responses (Pescatori et al., 1993; Wieder et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is based on citations to previous work on mammals.

claim: This signal is sent to lumbar spinothalamic (LSt) neurons in the spinal cord.
source: This signal is sent to lumbar spinothalamic (LSt) neurons in the spinal cord (Truitt and Coolen, 2002).
evidence: The claim is based on a citation to previous work on mammals.

claim: LSt cells then signal the neurons that control the emission and expulsion phases of ejaculation.
source: LSt cells then signal the neurons that control the emission and expulsion phases of ejaculation.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of mammalian ejaculation circuits.

claim: C. elegans ejaculatory circuitry is similarly set up to mammalian ejaculatory circuitry.
source: C. elegans ejaculatory circuitry is similarly set up (Figure 10)
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparisons between C. elegans and mammalian ejaculation circuits.
